## Methods

Fabrication of acoustically actuated antennas:
In the process of fabricating the three distinct devices, namely the FBAR-PE, HBAR-PE and HBAR-ME μ-antennas, a standardized procedure was followed to ensure consistency and precision in the manufacturing process. For detailed information, please refer to Supplementary Fig. S4. We initiated the process by creating a cavity pattern through the etching of a high-resistivity silicon substrate. Subsequently, a deposition of phosphor-silicon glass (PSG) was carried out employing the low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD) method. Following this, we polished the substrate surface utilizing chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) techniques. Then, an AlN seed layer and a bottom electrode composed of Mo were deposited through magnetron sputtering. Subsequently, the seed layer and bottom electrode underwent a patterning procedure facilitated by photolithograph and ICP etching. Continuing with the procedure, we sequentially deposited the AlScN piezoelectric layer, the Mo top electrode, and the AlN protective layer using magnetron sputtering techniques. Subsequently, the top electrode was patterned by photolithograph and ICP etching, requiring an etching in both the protective layer and the top electrode. Following this, the protective layer was etched to expose the contact pads of the top electrode. In the subsequent step, the AlScN piezoelectric layer underwent etching to create a via to the bottom electrode. Finally, we finished the process by forming the gold GSG (ground-signal-ground) electrode pad through a procedure involving photolithography, electron beam evaporation, and a lift-off process.

For the FBAR-PE μ-antenna, the fabrication began with cavity release using hydrofluoric acid, followed by the formation of the ZnO layer through photolithography, magnetron sputtering, and lift-off processes. In contrast, the fabrication of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna omitted the cavity release step and directly proceeded to patterned ZnO deposition. The HBAR-ME μ-antenna followed a notably different process: no top electrode or protective layer was deposited. Instead, after the formation of Au GSG electrodes, FeGaB was patterned using photolithography, sputtering, and lift-off. For both the PE and ME μ-antennas based on the HBAR structure, the wafer backside was mechanically thinned to 200 μm and polished using CMP after device fabrication to form the acoustic reflection interface.

Film deposition and characterization:
The ZnO material was deposited using a magnetron sputtering process with a Zn target under an oxygen atmosphere. This process yielded a ZnO material with a piezoelectric coefficient (d ) of 11 pm/V and a full width at half 33 maximum (FWHM) of 0.61 degrees. For the FeGaB material, a co-sputtering method was employed, involving a Fe Ga target and a B target. The FeGaB film was deposited in three segments, with a 15 nm Al O layer sputtered 0.8 0.2 2 3 after each ~200 nm of FeGaB deposition, yielding a total multilayer thickness of ~645 nm. The primary objective of this deposition was to reduce the conductivity of the magnetostrictive material. The coercive field of the FeGaB magnetostrictive material obtained was less than 0.1 mT.

Calculation of antenna properties:
The antenna gain (G ) is determined using the comparison method, given by the formula PE
G PE = G R + S 2 1 ,P E - S 2 1 ,R .
Here, G represents the gain of the reference antenna (Supplementary Fig. S20) at the resonance frequency of the R PE μ-antenna, while S and S are the transmission coefficients of the PE μ-antenna and the reference antenna, 21,PE 21,R respectively, at the resonance frequency. The Q factor of the PE μ-antenna is extracted from its reflection coefficient (S ) using the group delay method: 22
Q = \omega \cdot group delay (S 22) / (1 - |S 22|^2). The bandwidth of the antenna (FBW ) PE can be calculated by substituting the 3dB bandwidth of the PE μ-antennas, denoted as ∆f, into the equation FBW PE = f / f , where f is the resonant frequency. For the PE μ-antennas based on the FBAR structure, the resonant a a frequency bandwidths were measured to be 0.92% at 1.85 GHz and 1.02% at 3.91 GHz. This wide antenna bandwidth is attributed to the improved electromechanical coupling coefficient of the Sc-doped AlScN compared to AlN. In contrast, the HBAR-based PE μ-antenna exhibited a narrower single resonant frequency bandwidth of only 0.19%. This characteristic makes it more suitable for applications requiring high-Q narrowband antennas, precise measurement of frequency shifts such as wireless sensing.

Mason circuit model:
The Mason equivalent circuit model was developed to analyze the electrical properties of the PE μ-antenna. The circuit consists of layers arranged from top to bottom: the radiating layer, protective layer, top electrode, piezoelectric layer, bottom electrode, and seed layer. In this model, the characteristic acoustic impedance (Z) is defined as Z = E \cdot \rho, where E, , and β represent the Young's modulus, density, and acoustic propagation constant of the acoustic layer, respectively. The ZnO radiation layer is represented as an acoustic layer. Due to the piezoelectric effect, the acoustic impedance of the ZnO is modified accordingly to Z ra = (c E3 3 + e 23 3 / \epsilon S3 3) \cdot \rho. Additionally,  = \beta \cdot l , with l being the thickness of the acoustic layer. The piezoelectric layer is treated as a transformer circuit responsible for converting mechanical energy and electric one. Key parameters include k 2t = e 23 3 / (\epsilon S3 3 \cdot c E3 3), the static capacitance C 0 = \epsilon S3 3 \cdot A / d, the electromechanical coupling coefficient and the characteristic acoustic impedance of the piezoelectric layer Z pe = (c E3 3 + e 23 3 / \epsilon S3 3) \cdot \rho, where A is the FBAR effective region area and d is the thickness of the piezoelectric layer. Moreover, , S3 3  , e 3 3 and c E3 3 represent the piezoelectric layer's density, dielectric constant, piezoelectricity coefficient, and stiffness factor, respectively.

Finite element modeling of PE μ-antenna:
We developed a 3D finite element model with an active region area matching the device's structure in COMSOL (COMSOL Multiphysics 6.2). The simulations were conducted utilizing the Electrostatics and Solid Mechanics modules, with the incorporation of Piezoelectric Multiphysics field modules applied to the AlScN and ZnO layers. A voltage signal with an amplitude of 10 mV was applied to both the lower surface of the upper electrode and the upper surface of the lower electrode. To minimize the impact of transverse parasitic modes, the device was enclosed by a perfectly matched layer. In the simulations, a cell with an area of 11 μm2, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S6, was configured with layers the same as the antenna's structure. Periodic boundary conditions were implemented at the four boundaries (front, back, left, and right) of this cell. In the 2D simulation of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna, as depicted in Fig. 4a, the cavity beneath the AlN seed layer was filled with PSG to create the HBAR structure without the need for a cavity structure. Detailed material parameters for the layers employed in the simulations can be found in Supplementary Note 5.

Measurements:
(1) RF characterization: The S-parameters were measured using vector network analyzers (E5080B, Keysight, USA; ZNLE3, Rohde & Schwarz, Germany) according to measurement requirements, after standard short–open–load–through (SOLT) calibration. For antenna gain measurements, a horn antenna with known gain and the PE μ-antenna under test were connected to the calibrated ports of the VNA. The PE μ-antenna was contacted using a GSG probe on an RF probe station. The output power of VNA port was set to −10 dBm, and measurements were conducted at varying antenna separation distances. The impedance characteristics of the PE μ-antenna were converted from its reflection coefficient (S ). 22
(2) Wireless temperature sensing evaluation: The temperature response of the wireless sensing unit was evaluated using a wireless temperature sensing setup. The unit was fixed on a programmable heating plate and heated to target temperatures. The VNA was used to connect the unit and the receiving antenna for recording the S-parameters. The VNA port output power was set to –10 dBm, and the frequency resolution was 14 kHz.
(3) Wireless strain sensing evaluation: The strain response of the wireless sensing unit was characterized using a wireless strain sensing setup. The unit was bonded to a strain plate made of TC4 titanium alloy using strain gauge adhesive. To calibrate the applied strain, a resistive strain gauge was attached to the same plate. The unit was positioned adjacent to the strain gauge, aligned with its center, to ensure consistent strain exposure. The VNA was used to acquire the S-parameters by connecting the unit and the receiving antenna. The VNA port output power was set to –10 dBm, and the frequency resolution was 2.5 kHz.

### Reviewer 1

The authors present an acoustic-resonance-driven piezoelectric microantenna based on film and high-overtone bulk acoustic resonator (FBAR/HBAR) structures, with a total footprint of 0.019 mm². They demonstrate its wireless sensing capability with a transmission distance of up to one meter. This work addresses two fundamental challenges in wireless sensing: antenna miniaturization and the integration of sensing functionality within an ultracompact form factor. The research establishes a scalable and highly miniaturized device platform that ranks among the smallest wireless sensing units with an integrated antenna reported to date. As such, it is likely to attract significant interest in the fields of MEMS, wireless communication, and microscale sensing.
In my view, this represents a notable achievement in tackling long-standing challenges pursued by researchers and engineers. The technology holds promises for broad implications and applications across various domains, including industry, biomedicine (particularly implants), and space exploration. I would recommend consideration for publication in Nature Communications, pending the consideration for the following technical points.
1. The authors need to ensure consistent terminology for the μ-antenna throughout the manuscript. The terms FBAR/HBAR-PE antenna and FBAR/HBAR-PE μ-antenna are used interchangeably (e.g., lines 89, 307, and 311). A single, consistent form would be better and clearer to readers.
2. Fig. S2 and Fig. S3 show the characterization of the piezoelectric materials, but no comparison with previous studies is provided to indicate the material performance.
3. In Fig. 3b, the antenna S22 exhibits two resonance peaks, but only one resonance produces an observable electromagnetic radiation peak in Fig. 3d. The reason for this discrepancy is not explained, and its impact on antenna performance should be discussed.
4. The HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits a longer transmission distance than the FBAR-PE μ-antenna (Fig. 4), but the manuscript does not clarify how this improvement correlates with the increase in Q factor.
5. The FBAR-PE μ-antenna could operate at both the first and second resonance modes. In Fig. 4, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna shows resonance enhancement at the first FBAR mode. Can it also operate at the second FBAR mode and generate the corresponding electromagnetic radiation for wireless sensing?
6. Both the HBAR-ME and HBAR-PE μ-antennas are built on the same HBAR platform, but the manuscript does not provide a rationale for why their performance can be directly compared.
7. In Fig. S12b, the comparison with Fig. 4d is presented, and the manuscript states that “the use of a PSG layer with lower acoustic impedance results in more effective reflection of acoustic stress back into the ZnO+FBAR region.” This statement does not explain the underlying mechanism. The authors should clarify the role of the PSG layer and how it influences acoustic stress reflection within the device.
8. The authors demonstrate that the HBAR-based PE μ-antenna exhibits wireless sensing functionality, with the wireless transmission enabled by the antenna itself. However, it is not clear which parts of the structure are responsible for the sensing function.

### Reviewer 2

Miniaturized on-chip sensor units with integrated antennas remain a key technical challenge in modern microscale sensing, owing to the stringent constraints on device footprint and the demand for reliable wireless operation in complex environments such as wearable electronics, compact industrial systems, and distributed sensor networks. Critical design considerations include achieving antenna miniaturization without compromising sensing performance-ideally through vertical integration, establishing theoretical guidance for the design of nanoantennas capable of long-range wireless transmission. Despite significant progress in microscale sensing technologies, it remains difficult to simultaneously achieve compact device dimensions and high-performance wireless operation.
The manuscript reports a microantenna and a wireless microsensor with an active area of merely 0.02 mm2, effectively addressing many of the aforementioned challenges. The ultracompact sensor unit demonstrates both temperature and strain sensing capabilities, with a remarkable transmission distance of up to one meter among the best results reported to date. Furthermore, the integrated sensor unit exhibits excellent scalability, suggesting strong potential for diverse application scenarios. Compared with magnetoelectric (ME) film-based antennas, ZnO piezoelectric (PE) thin-film nanoantennas offer advantages in terms of material availability, ease of fabrication, and performance. Overall, this study lays an important foundation for the next generation of wireless micro-sensing systems.
I would recommend publication in Nature Communications after the authors carefully address the following points:
(1) HBARs exhibit multiple resonance peaks with high Q-factors. Can each resonance mode be utilized for sensing or wireless transmission? Do all peaks exhibit comparable performance? How can users select the most appropriate mode for specific applications? Moreover, is there a strategy to enhance the dominant resonance (e.g., increasing its Q-factor) while suppressing parasitic modes, thereby concentrating the acoustic energy for longer transmission distances? In short, could the HBAR-based nanoantenna design be further optimized for higher performance?
(2) For large-scale fabrication, what are the observed variations in resonance frequency and Q-factor among fabricated HBARs? How do these variations influence the performance consistency of the nanoantennas and sensor units? The authors are encouraged to comment on the uniformity of ZnO-based antennas and HBARs both across a single wafer and between different wafers.
(3) Although the demonstrated transmission distance reaches up to one meter, could the authors discuss possible strategies to extend the wireless communication range further? Insights into design, material, or system-level improvements that could enable longer-distance operation would be valuable.
(4) While FBARs and HBARs have been demonstrated for temperature and strain sensing, they are, in principle, capable of detecting multiple physical parameters. What additional sensing functionalities could be realized with this microsensor platform? Furthermore, could the authors comment on the feasibility of adapting the proposed device for biomedical or implantable applications, which would significantly broaden its impact?
(5) Figures S2 and S3 present the characterization of the piezoelectric materials. The manuscript would be strengthened if these results were compared with those from previous studies. Any observed improvement in ZnO film quality could directly enhance the overall performance of the sensor/antenna unit.
(6) PSG is used as an acoustic reflector, though it increases fabrication complexity. Is the inclusion of the PSG layer essential? How would the device performance change if a silicon substrate were used directly as the acoustic reflector?
(7) Although ZnO offers relatively good piezoelectric performance, its piezoelectric coefficient (d33) is lower than that of some alternative materials. Would it be feasible to employ higher-performance materials such as PZT with larger d33 and electromechanical coupling coefficients? What are the key challenges or limitations that prevent the integration of such materials into the nanoantenna design?

Wireless sensing systems enable real-time, non-contact monitoring for next-generation intelligent platforms. Ideal wireless sensing systems feature compact, low power consumption, and long communication range. Here we report a miniaturized wireless sensing system with an in tegrated acoustic-resonance-driven piezoelectric microantenna (PE μ-antenna) with a 0.0196 mm2 active arLea. The PE μ-antenna integrated on a film bulk acoustic resonator (FBAR) achieves dual-frequency radiation at 1.85 GHz and 3.91 GHz with gains of –32.96 dBi and –20.5 dBi, respectively. The μ-antennas achieve over four orders of magnitude radiation efficiency enhancement and volume reduction compared with exiAsting piezoelectric transmitters. We further extend this approach to high-overtone bulk acoustic resonators with high quality factors for wireless sensing. The system enables temperature and strain sensing with a transmission range up to 1 m, demonstrating state-of-the-art miniaturization and transmission performance among wireless sensing systems. This work establishes a scalable platform for ultracompact wireless sensors and communication nodes in biomedical, wearable, and aerospace applications.

## Introduction

In diverse fields, from wearable and implantable devices to the Internet of Things (IoT) and aerospace1-4, there is an urgent demand for compact, high-performance wireless sensing systems that can operate under stringent constraints on size, power, and integration. However, as a key enabler of wireless communication, conventional design of antennas is fundamentally constrained by the operating wavelength and antennas occupy substantial system space, hindering miniaturization of the systems. Although alternative signal-transmission strategies based on magnetic, optical, or acoustic mechanisms have been explored5-8, they often suffer from limitations in terms of application scope, communication range, and reliability. As such, direct miniaturization of the anStenna itself remains one of the most effective and universal pathways toward truly compact sensing platforms9. Furthermore, integrating sensing functionality directly into the antenna structurPe not only eliminates additional interfaces and interconnects, but also reduces system size and Npower consumption, and enhances overall system integration10-12, offering a viable route towar d highly compact and efficient wireless microsensors. Consequently, it is necessary not only to aLchieve antenna miniaturization, but also to effectively integrate miniaturized antennas with sensors to advance wireless sensing technology.

To overcome the wavelength-imposed size limitations of conventional antennas, researchers have recently explored miniaturAized antenna concepts based on acoustic-driven electromagnetic radiation. The first class of size-reduced antennas comprises piezoelectric transmitters, where mechanical vibrations generate oscillating electric-dipole radiation through piezoelectric coupling13-17. To date, the piezoelectric transmitters predominantly rely on bulk materials such as lithium niobate and lead zirconate titanate (PZT) but have the centimeter sizes18-27, restricting their operation to the ultralow frequency (ULF) or very low frequency (VLF) ranges with extremely low radiation efficiencies (<10–5 %). They are not suitable for the integration into microsystems for practical applications due to the bulky dimensions and the extremely low radiation efficiencies. The second class of miniaturized antennas is the magnetoelectric (ME) antennas, which exploit magnetostrictive/piezoelectric heterostructures for efficient magnetic-to-electric signal conversion28-33. By integrating ME microantennas on acoustic resonators, efficient conversion of acoustic energy into electromagnetic radiation has been demonstrated across a broad spectrum—from the VLF band up to the RF range34-39. However, their performance remains limited by the available material systems and fixed resonant modes, resulting in limited radiation efficiency, low quality (Q) factor, and poor scalability40-47, and integrated high-sensitivity compact wireless sensing system is yet to be demonstrated.

High-overtone bulk acoustic resonators (HBARs) provide a compelling pathway to overcome these limitations. HBARs possess multiple high-overtone resonances with ultrahigh Q, excellent frequency stability, and ultralow energy dissipation. These characteristics have enabled their use in high-sensitivity sensing48, integrated photonic devices49, and microwave-photonics transducers50. In addition, HBARs are inherently compatible with microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) fabrication process and are suitable for chip-scale integration, making them an ideal platform for tight coupling of antenna radiation and sensing functionalities within a single device.

Here, we propose a piezoelectric thin film radiation platform at the micro/nanoscale and demonstrate a wireless sensing approach using bulk acoustic resonatoPr sensors integrated with a PE microantenna (PE μ-antenna). To verify the validity and feasibility of Nthe proposed radiation model, we design and fabricate a PE μ-antenna integrated on a film bulk acoust ic resonator (named as FBAR-PE μ-antenna). The FBAR-PE μ-antenna with an area of merely 0.019L6 mm2 operates in dual-frequency modes at 1.85 and 3.91 GHz, having gains of –32.96 dBi and –20.5 dBi respectively. This design achieves a greater than four orders of magnitude radiation efficiency enhancement and volume reduction compared to the state-of-the-art piezoelectric transmitters.A We further extend this concept to high-Q HBAR structures to develop the PE μ-antenna integrated on an HBAR (HBAR-PE μ-antenna), enabling higher-efficiency transmission of resonance-coupled electromagnetic waves. The HBAR sensor unit with the integrated PE μ-antenna has the same total active area of 0.0196 mm2 and achieves sensitivities of –27.8 ppm/°C and –0.13 ppm/μɛ for temperature and strain wireless sensing, respectively, at a 1 m transmission distance. These results demonstrate a class of integrated, compact piezoelectric antennas that fuse wireless transmission and sensing together, offering a promising path toward highly integrated, low-power wireless sensor systems in diverse fields.

## Results

2.1 FBAR-PE μ-antenna design and radiation analysis
PE μ-antennas can be coupled with acoustic waves in various acoustic resonators to achieve the transmission and reception of electromagnetic waves. For simplicity, we first use FBAR with a simpler structure and operation mechanism to investigate the radiation behavior of the PE μ-antenna as HBAR has a similar structure to that of FBAR. We designate this μ-antenna structure as FBAR-PE μ-antenna (see Supplementary Fig. S1 for the structure details). The FBAR device consists of a molybdenum (Mo, 100 nm) - scandium alloyed aluminum nitride (AlScN, 350 nm) - Mo (150 nm) sandwich structure. The Mo electrodes were used owing to their high acoustic impedance and low acoustic loss. The AlScN material with a 9.6% was chosen for its combined merits of high acoustic velocity and high electromechanical coupling coefficient. To facilitate film growth and prevent oxidation of the Mo electrodes, an ultrathin aluminum nitride (AlN) film of 30 nm thickness was utilized as the seed layer beneath the bottom Mo electrode and an AlN layer of 150 nm thickness as the protective layer over the top Mo electrode, respectively. A ZnO film (1050 nm) possessing a pronounced (002) crystal orientation was sputter-deposited onto the AlN protective layer to serve as the PE μ-antenna’s radiating layer (Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3 for the AlScN and ZnOP properties). These layers were deposited on a silicon (Si) substrate and patterned sequentially, and the cavity was produced by removing the phosphosilicate glass (PSG) sacrificial layer (Su pplementary Fig. S4 for a detailed fabrication process for the FBAR and the PE μ-antenna). It shoulLd be noted that the FBARs were fabricated by a standard 8-inch CMOS compatible process with the PE μ-antenna fabricated afterwards at the Micro-Nano Fabrication Center of Zhejiang University separately.

Figure 1a illustrates Athe FBAR PE μ-antenna’s working principle. When RF signals are applied between the top and bottom electrodes, the AlScN piezoelectric layer produces acoustic waves via the inverse piezoelectric effect. At specific frequencies that coincide with the thickness-mode resonances of the FBAR stack, standing acoustic waves are established along the thickness direction of the FBAR with a ZnO PE layer on top. These standing waves exert periodic stress on the ZnO layer of the PE μ-antenna, inducing axial deformation along the c-axis. This periodic deformation of the ZnO layer leads to a continuous rotation of the polarization vector, resembling the dynamic behavior of an oscillating electric dipole, enabling the radiation of electromagnetic waves (i.e. the transmission) with the same frequencies. In the receiving process, the electric field component of an incident electromagnetic wave couples into the ZnO layer of the PE μ-antenna and induces acoustic waves via the piezoelectric effect. If the frequency of the incident wave matches the FBAR’s resonance modes, acoustic standing waves are formed across the multilayer stack. The standing waves in the AlScN layer are then converted into an electrical signal at the electrodes through the piezoelectric effect.

2.3 PE μ-antenna based on HBAR structure
Having established the basic operation of the PE μ-antenna on an FBAR, we extend our investigation to PE μ-antennas operating in high-overtone modes which exhibit considerably higher Q factors which are promising for the development of high-performance miniaturized wireless sensors. The HBAR-PE μ-antenna structure is shown in Fig. 4a. Apart from the PSG layer under the FBAR stack, which serves as an effective acoustic reflection interface (Supplementary Fig. S12), the film-stack configuration and the top ZnO layer remain identical to those of the FBAR-PE μ-antenna. This implies that HBAR-PE μ-antenna operates in high-overtone modes, while having an inherently built-in FBAR structure with a corresponding resonant frequency band. This design also greatly enhances structural stability and robustness compared to FBARs due to the elimination of the air cavity underneath. Its fabrication process resembles that of the FBAR device but skips the step of etching the PSG layer to release the FBAR structure (see Supplementary Fig. S4), and the back of the Si substrate is polished to a thickness of 200 μm by chemical-mechanical polishing process. The HBAR-PE μ-antenna also has the same active area (0.0196 mm2) as that of FBAR-PE μ-antenna.

Figure 4b presents the impedance characteristics of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. To compare and optimize performance, we fabricated HBARs using AlScN layers with Sc concentrations of 9.6% and 20% respectively. The μ-antenna operates in the high-overtone thickness resonant modes of the HBAR structure, characterized by a free spectral range (FSR) of 17 MHz (f = v a / 2d total = 17 MHz) between adjacent resonance peaks, here, d represents the total thickness of the HBAR structure in the active total region. The Q-values of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna are 1006 for the HBAR-PE μ-antennas with 9.6% Sc content and 859 for those with 20% Sc content, which are much higher than the Q (~176 for the first modes) of the FBAR-PE μ-antennas. Figure 4b also shows the equivalent circuit impedance of the built-in FBAR structure within the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. Notably, the impedance profile of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits an envelope peak appearing at the resonance frequency of the first mode of its built-in FBAR structure, indicating a coupling between the two structures in terms of their resonance characteristics. Consequently, the high-Q HBAR structure introduces multiple resonance modes within the operating band of the first mode of the built-in FBAR, thereby extending the usable spectral range and providing a resonance-enhanced regime that significantly improves the Q-factors of PE μ-antennas.

The resonance-enhanced effect observed in Fig. 4b can be interpreted from both physical and circuit perspectives. Physically, Fig. 4c displays the normalized two-dimensional stress distribution in the active region of the antenna within the operating band of the built-in FBAR. At the in-band resonance, the acoustic wave generated by the FBAR structure propagates along the y-direction, reflects within the underneath substrate, and forms a standing wave. Simultaneously, the active region of the built-in FBAR structure operates in its first mode, exhibiting a half-wavelength standing wave distribution. Figure 4d compares the stress between resonance points in and out the operating band. Within the operating band, the built-in FBAR structure forms a half-wavelength standing wave, and the substrate’s stress is lower than that of the first mode standing wave at the top, demonstrating the resonance enhancement provided by the built-in FBAR structure. In contrast, outside the operating band, the built-in FBAR structure does not operate in its resonance mode, and the stress level in the PE μ-antenna decreases by about two orders of magnitude, reflecting the absence of the resonance enhancement effect. From the circuit perspective, the Mason equivalent circuit of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna (Supplementary Fig. S5) can be described by two parallel elements: the HBAR structure and its built-in FBAR structure. Consequently, under the influence of FBAR resonance, the HBAR device exhibits an envelope peak near the thickness resonance frequency of the FBAR, consistent with the physical interpretation.

Simulation results confirm that the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits high Q-factors, with stress significantly enhanced at resonance points within the operating band due to the resonance enhancement effect. To validate this effect experimentally, we measured the HBAR-PE μ-antenna using the same gain comparison method as for the FBAR-PE μ-antenna. Figures 4e and 4f show the S parameters for the μ-antennas incorporating AlScN layers with Sc concentrations of 9.6% and 20%, respectively. The corresponding peak reflection coefficients are –2.21 dB and –8.96 dB, indicating improved impedance matching with higher Sc content. Figures 4g and 4h display the corresponding S and S curves, which 21 12 fully overlap. Within the operating band, the transmission coefficients reach their maximum levels, with each S and S peak aligning with that of the S resonance frequencies of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. 21 12 22 These results indicate that the HBAR-PE μ-antenna follows the same acoustic-electromagnetic radiation conversion principle as the FBAR-PE μ-antenna in both transmission and reception. The resonance enhancement effect drives the built-in FBAR structure to operate in the first resonant mode at multiple in-band resonance points, increasing the stress in the ZnO layer and thereby maximizing the radiation efficiency.

The measured peak gains of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna are –28.98 dBi for the 9.6% Sc device and –26.23 dBi for the 20% Sc device, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 4 - 6.7 dBi over the FBAR-PE μ-antenna in its first mode. Since all the in-band resonances correspond to the first mode of the FBAR-PE μ-antenna, the radiation efficiencies can be evaluated based on the radiation characteristics of the first mode of FBAR, which are 0.080% and 0.156% for the 9.6% and 20% Sc devices, respectively. Consistently, the measured radiation patterns exhibit the oscillating electric-dipole characteristics of this mode (Supplementary Fig. S13), further validating the efficiency estimation. These results further confirm that the resonance enhancement effect facilitates more efficient acoustic-to- electromagnetic radiation energy conversion within the operating band. In addition, the central frequency of the operating band shifts from 2.06 GHz to 1.97 GHz, due to the reduced longitudinal acoustic velocity in the AlScN layer with higher Sc content60. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S14, the HBAR–PE μ-antenna also exhibits resonance enhancement in the second operating band, with stress again concentrated in the FBAR region. However, at these higher frequencies, the acoustic wavelength is shortened, leading to an increased number of standing waves in the substrate and reduced in-band resonance confinement. Coupled with enhanced boundary scattering and out-of-band energy leakage, these effects collectively result in a substantial reduction of the Q-factor. Consequently, the radiation gain and overall radiation efficiency in the second band of the built-in FBAR are much smaller compared to those of the first mode, rendering this band unsuitable for effective wireless signal transmission. Therefore, for practical wireless sensing applications, only the first band is employed as the operative mode of the device.

Figure 4i further demonstrates that, as the test distance increases from 10 cm to 1 m, the transmission coefficient peaks remain discernible but are reduced by an average of ~15 dB. This trend aligns with the expected free-space path loss of electromagnetic waves. The extended transmission range is attributed to the high Q factor of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna and the narrow bandwidth associated with its single resonance mode. By reducing energy dissipation and concentrating the acoustic–electrical conversion within a narrow resonance bandwidth, the high-Q HBAR structure enhances radiation intensity and improves the signal-to-noise ratio, thereby enabling more efficient long-range transmission.

ME μ-antennas have been studied by a few groups, and demonstrated its good potential for applications. To directly compare the performance of our PE μ-antennas with that of the ME μ-antennas, we also fabricated ME μ-antennas integrated on the same high-Q HBAR platform (HBAR-ME μ-antennas; the HBAR platform is characterized in Supplementary Fig. S15) to ensure identical structural configuration and acoustic propagation paths, and to minimize variations in residual stress across different material stacks. The HBAR-ME μ-antennas utilize FeGaB as the magnetostrictive layer, which exhibits a low coercive field (<0.1 mT), indicating favorable soft magnetic properties (Supplementary Fig. S16). As shown in Supplementary Fig. S17, the measured gain of the HBAR-ME μ-antennas is, on average, 3–4 dBi lower than that of their HBAR-PE counterparts, confirming the higher radiation efficiency achieved by the HBAR-PE μ-antennas. It should be noted that the resonant frequencies (Supplementary Fig. S17) of the built-in FBAR with ME antennas are higher than those (Fig. 4) of the built-in FBAR with PE antennas. This is attributed to the thinner (~645 nm) FeGaB layer with a low acoustic velocity, in contrast to the thicker (~1 μm) but high-velocity ZnO layer.

Figure 4j shows the relationship between radiation efficiency and antenna volume for the ME and PE μ-antennas with various sizes reported so far and our FBAR-PE and HBAR-PE μ-antennas. It is evident that the PE μ-antennas reduce the antenna size by 4-5 orders of magnitude and enhance radiation efficiency over 4 orders of magnitude compared to conventional piezoelectric transmitters. Notably, despite their significantly smaller size, our PE μ-antennas ultimately achieve a radiation efficiency better than or comparable to those of the state-of-the-art ME antennas34, 38, 41. This result is consistent with the comparative analysis between FBAR-PE, HBAR-PE, and ME μ-antennas, further validating the advantage of the proposed PE μ-antennas.

2.4 Wireless sensing by HBAR sensor with an integrated PE μ-antenna
The HBAR-PE μ-antenna has a higher Q factor than its FBAR-PE counterpart, enabling selectivity for frequencies with superior radiation efficiency and enhancing sensitivity for sensing. Therefore, we utilized HBAR-PE μ-antennas for wireless sensing demonstration in this work. The experimental setup for temperature and stress monitoring using HBAR sensor with integrated PE μ-antenna is illustrated in Fig. 5a. The HBAR structure, like the FBAR61, 62, is sensitive to external physical stimuli such as temperature and mechanical strain, with its frequency variation governed by the properties of the substrate materials as discussed in Supplementary Note 2. These perturbations alter the acoustic wave velocity and propagation path within the resonant cavity, resulting in a measurable shift in resonance frequency, as reflected in the S 22 parameter. As discussed earlier, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits peak radiation at resonance frequencies within the operating band of the built-in FBAR. The transmission coefficient reaches its maximum at frequencies that coincide with the μ-antenna’s resonance, establishing a one-to-one correspondence. Therefore, any shift in resonant frequency induced by stimuli will directly manifest as a shift in the transmission coefficient peak, which can be remotely detected by monitoring the position of the corresponding S or S peak at the receiving end.

For wireless temperature sensing, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna was placed on a programmable hot plate for temperature control and calibration. The horn antenna was placed at a distance away from the sensor unit (Supplementary Fig. S18). As shown in Fig. 5b for a test distance of 20 cm, the resonance peak of the μ-antenna’s S parameter exhibits a linear shift with temperature in the range of 30 ℃ to 200 ℃, with a sensitivity of –27.8 ppm/℃. Correspondingly, the peak frequencies of the received S and S signals 21 12 for the same test distance also follow a linear relationship with temperature (Fig. 5c), consistent with the S response, confirming that the PE μ-antenna can reliably transmit sensing information wirelessly. We calculated the deviation between the transmission coefficients (S and S ) shift and the S frequency 21 12 22 shift, and converted this into a temperature error using the linear relation (Figs. 5d and 5e). As the wireless transmission distance increases from 20 cm to 1 m, the sensing error increases slightly, but remaining within ±2 ℃. This deterioration is attributed to the reduced signal strength and resultant lower signal-to-noise ratio at longer distances.

Similarly, we evaluated the HBAR-PE μ-antenna as a wireless strain sensor, with calibration provided by a commercial resistive strain gauge (Supplementary Fig. S19). As shown in Fig. 5f for a test distance of 20 cm, the S resonance peaks shift linearly with applied strain in the range of 0-1000 με, 22 with a sensitivity of –0.13 ppm/με. The strain sensitivity is rather lower compared to other techniques, and is attributed to both the weak strain dependence of silicon’s longitudinal acoustic velocity and the limited sensing area, which lacks sufficient length along the deformation direction. Although the overall frequency shift due to strain variation (~261 kHz) is relatively smaller for the 20cm distance test, the peak frequencies of the S and S signals at the receiver end remain discernable and are consistent with the 21 12 μ-antenna’s resonance shifts (Fig. 5g). The wireless strain sensing error, derived by converting frequency deviation into strain values (Figs. 5h and 5i), remain within ±65 με for transmission distances up to 1 m.

Importantly, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits negligible hysteresis under both the temperature and strain sensing conditions, indicating good linearity and repeatability. ## Methods

Fabrication of acoustically actuated antennas:
In the process of fabricating the three distinct devices, namely the FBAR-PE, HBAR-PE and HBAR-ME μ-antennas, a standardized procedure was followed to ensure consistency and precision in the manufacturing process. For detailed information, please refer to Supplementary Fig. S4. We initiated the process by creating a cavity pattern through the etching of a high-resistivity silicon substrate. Subsequently, a deposition of phosphor-silicon glass (PSG) was carried out employing the low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD) method. Following this, we polished the substrate surface utilizing chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) techniques. Then, an AlN seed layer and a bottom electrode composed of Mo were deposited through magnetron sputtering. Subsequently, the seed layer and bottom electrode underwent a patterning procedure facilitated by photolithograph and ICP etching. Continuing with the procedure, we sequentially deposited the AlScN piezoelectric layer, the Mo top electrode, and the AlN protective layer using magnetron sputtering techniques. Subsequently, the top electrode was patterned by photolithograph and ICP etching, requiring an etching in both the protective layer and the top electrode. Following this, the protective layer was etched to expose the contact pads of the top electrode. In the subsequent step, the AlScN piezoelectric layer underwent etching to create a via to the bottom electrode. Finally, we finished the process by forming the gold GSG (ground-signal-ground) electrode pad through a procedure involving photolithography, electron beam evaporation, and a lift-off process.

For the FBAR-PE μ-antenna, the fabrication began with cavity release using hydrofluoric acid, followed by the formation of the ZnO layer through photolithography, magnetron sputtering, and lift-off processes. In contrast, the fabrication of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna omitted the cavity release step and directly proceeded to patterned ZnO deposition. The HBAR-ME μ-antenna followed a notably different process: no top electrode or protective layer was deposited. Instead, after the formation of Au GSG electrodes, FeGaB was patterned using photolithography, sputtering, and lift-off. For both the PE and ME μ-antennas based on the HBAR structure, the wafer backside was mechanically thinned to 200 μm and polished using CMP after device fabrication to form the acoustic reflection interface.

Film deposition and characterization:
The ZnO material was deposited using a magnetron sputtering process with a Zn target under an oxygen atmosphere. This process yielded a ZnO material with a piezoelectric coefficient (d ) of 11 pm/V and a full width at half 33 maximum (FWHM) of 0.61 degrees. For the FeGaB material, a co-sputtering method was employed, involving a Fe Ga target and a B target. The FeGaB film was deposited in three segments, with a 15 nm Al O layer sputtered 0.8 0.2 2 3 after each ~200 nm of FeGaB deposition, yielding a total multilayer thickness of ~645 nm. The primary objective of this deposition was to reduce the conductivity of the magnetostrictive material. The coercive field of the FeGaB magnetostrictive material obtained was less than 0.1 mT.

The Mason equivalent circuit model was developed to analyze the electrical properties of the PE μ-antenna. The circuit consists of layers arranged from top to bottom: the radiating layer, protective layer, top electrode, piezoelectric layer, bottom electrode, and seed layer. In this model, the characteristic acoustic impedance (Z) is defined as Z = E \cdot \rho, where E, , and β represent the Young's modulus, density, and acoustic propagation constant of the acoustic layer, respectively. The ZnO radiation layer is represented as an acoustic layer. Due to the piezoelectric effect, the acoustic impedance of the ZnO is modified accordingly to Z ra = (c E3 3 + e 23 3 / \epsilon S3 3) \cdot \rho. Additionally,  = \beta \cdot l , with l being the thickness of the acoustic layer. The piezoelectric layer is treated as a transformer circuit responsible for converting mechanical energy and electric one. Key parameters include k 2t = e 23 3 / (\epsilon S3 3 \cdot c E3 3), the static capacitance C 0 = \epsilon S3 3 \cdot A / d, the electromechanical coupling coefficient and the characteristic acoustic impedance of the piezoelectric layer Z pe = (c E3 3 + e 23 3 / \epsilon S3 3) \cdot \rho, where A is the FBAR effective region area and d is the thickness of the piezoelectric layer. Moreover, , S3 3  , e 3 3 and c E3 3 represent the piezoelectric layer's density, dielectric constant, piezoelectricity coefficient, and stiffness factor, respectively.

Finite element modeling of PE μ-antenna:
We developed a 3D finite element model with an active region area matching the device's structure in COMSOL (COMSOL Multiphysics 6.2). The simulations were conducted utilizing the Electrostatics and Solid Mechanics modules, with the incorporation of Piezoelectric Multiphysics field modules applied to the AlScN and ZnO layers. A voltage signal with an amplitude of 10 mV was applied to both the lower surface of the upper electrode and the upper surface of the lower electrode. To minimize the impact of transverse parasitic modes, the device was enclosed by a perfectly matched layer. In the simulations, a cell with an area of 11 μm2, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S6, was configured with layers the same as the antenna's structure. Periodic boundary conditions were implemented at the four boundaries (front, back, left, and right) of this cell. In the 2D simulation of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna, as depicted in Fig. 4a, the cavity beneath the AlN seed layer was filled with PSG to create the HBAR structure without the need for a cavity structure. Detailed material parameters for the layers employed in the simulations can be found in Supplementary Note 5.

Measurements:
(1) RF characterization: The S-parameters were measured using vector network analyzers (E5080B, Keysight, USA; ZNLE3, Rohde & Schwarz, Germany) according to measurement requirements, after standard short–open–load–through (SOLT) calibration. For antenna gain measurements, a horn antenna with known gain and the PE μ-antenna under test were connected to the calibrated ports of the VNA. The PE μ-antenna was contacted using a GSG probe on an RF probe station. The output power of VNA port was set to −10 dBm, and measurements were conducted at varying antenna separation distances. The impedance characteristics of the PE μ-antenna were converted from its reflection coefficient (S ). 22
(2) Wireless temperature sensing evaluation: The temperature response of the wireless sensing unit was evaluated using a wireless temperature sensing setup. The unit was fixed on a programmable heating plate and heated to target temperatures. The VNA was used to connect the unit and the receiving antenna for recording the S-parameters. The VNA port output power was set to –10 dBm, and the frequency resolution was 14 kHz.
(3) Wireless strain sensing evaluation: The strain response of the wireless sensing unit was characterized using a wireless strain sensing setup. The unit was bonded to a strain plate made of TC4 titanium alloy using strain gauge adhesive. To calibrate the applied strain, a resistive strain gauge was attached to the same plate. The unit was positioned adjacent to the strain gauge, aligned with its center, to ensure consistent strain exposure. The VNA was used to acquire the S-parameters by connecting the unit and the receiving antenna. The VNA port output power was set to –10 dBm, and the frequency resolution was 2.5 kHz.

## Introduction

In diverse fields, from wearable and implantable devices to the Internet of Things (IoT) and aerospace1-4, there is an urgent demand for compact, high-performance wireless sensing systems that can operate under stringent constraints on size, power, and integration. However, as a key enabler of wireless communication, conventional design of antennas is fundamentally constrained by the operating wavelength and antennas occupy substantial system space, hindering miniaturization of the systems. Although alternative signal-transmission strategies based on magnetic, optical, or acoustic mechanisms have been explored5-8, they often suffer from limitations in terms of application scope, communication range, and reliability. As such, direct miniaturization of the anStenna itself remains one of the most effective and universal pathways toward truly compact sensing platforms9. Furthermore, integrating sensing functionality directly into the antenna structurPe not only eliminates additional interfaces and interconnects, but also reduces system size and Npower consumption, and enhances overall system integration10-12, offering a viable route towar d highly compact and efficient wireless microsensors. Consequently, it is necessary not only to aLchieve antenna miniaturization, but also to effectively integrate miniaturized antennas with sensors to advance wireless sensing technology.

To overcome the wavelength-imposed size limitations of conventional antennas, researchers have recently explored miniaturAized antenna concepts based on acoustic-driven electromagnetic radiation. The first class of size-reduced antennas comprises piezoelectric transmitters, where mechanical vibrations generate oscillating electric-dipole radiation through piezoelectric coupling13-17. To date, the piezoelectric transmitters predominantly rely on bulk materials such as lithium niobate and lead zirconate titanate (PZT) but have the centimeter sizes18-27, restricting their operation to the ultralow frequency (ULF) or very low frequency (VLF) ranges with extremely low radiation efficiencies (<10–5 %). They are not suitable for the integration into microsystems for practical applications due to the bulky dimensions and the extremely low radiation efficiencies. The second class of miniaturized antennas is the magnetoelectric (ME) antennas, which exploit magnetostrictive/piezoelectric heterostructures for efficient magnetic-to-electric signal conversion28-33. By integrating ME microantennas on acoustic resonators, efficient conversion of acoustic energy into electromagnetic radiation has been demonstrated across a broad spectrum—from the VLF band up to the RF range34-39. However, their performance remains limited by the available material systems and fixed resonant modes, resulting in limited radiation efficiency, low quality (Q) factor, and poor scalability40-47, and integrated high-sensitivity compact wireless sensing system is yet to be demonstrated.

High-overtone bulk acoustic resonators (HBARs) provide a compelling pathway to overcome these limitations. HBARs possess multiple high-overtone resonances with ultrahigh Q, excellent frequency stability, and ultralow energy dissipation. These characteristics have enabled their use in high-sensitivity sensing48, integrated photonic devices49, and microwave-photonics transducers50. In addition, HBARs are inherently compatible with microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) fabrication process and are suitable for chip-scale integration, making them an ideal platform for tight coupling of antenna radiation and sensing functionalities within a single device.

This is because, for all odd-order resonant modes, the top and bottom surfaces of the resonator vibrate in opposite directions. 2.3 PE μ-antenna based on HBAR structure
Having established the basic operation of the PE μ-antenna on an FBAR, we extend our investigation to PE μ-antennas operating in high-overtone modes which exhibit considerably higher Q factors which are promising for the development of high-performance miniaturized wireless sensors. The HBAR-PE μ-antenna structure is shown in Fig. 4a. Apart from the PSG layer under the FBAR stack, which serves as an effective acoustic reflection interface (Supplementary Fig. S12), the film-stack configuration and the top ZnO layer remain identical to those of the FBAR-PE μ-antenna. This implies that HBAR-PE μ-antenna operates in high-overtone modes, while having an inherently built-in FBAR structure with a corresponding resonant frequency band. This design also greatly enhances structural stability and robustness compared to FBARs due to the elimination of the air cavity underneath. Its fabrication process resembles that of the FBAR device but skips the step of etching the PSG layer to release the FBAR structure (see Supplementary Fig. S4), and the back of the Si substrate is polished to a thickness of 200 μm by chemical-mechanical polishing process. The HBAR-PE μ-antenna also has the same active area (0.0196 mm2) as that of FBAR-PE μ-antenna.

Figure 4b presents the impedance characteristics of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. To compare and optimize performance, we fabricated HBARs using AlScN layers with Sc concentrations of 9.6% and 20% respectively. The μ-antenna operates in the high-overtone thickness resonant modes of the HBAR structure, characterized by a free spectral range (FSR) of 17 MHz (f = v a / 2d total = 17 MHz) between adjacent resonance peaks, here, d represents the total thickness of the HBAR structure in the active total region. The Q-values of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna are 1006 for the HBAR-PE μ-antennas with 9.6% Sc content and 859 for those with 20% Sc content, which are much higher than the Q (~176 for the first modes) of the FBAR-PE μ-antennas. Figure 4b also shows the equivalent circuit impedance of the built-in FBAR structure within the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. Notably, the impedance profile of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits an envelope peak appearing at the resonance frequency of the first mode of its built-in FBAR structure, indicating a coupling between the two structures in terms of their resonance characteristics. Consequently, the high-Q HBAR structure introduces multiple resonance modes within the operating band of the first mode of the built-in FBAR, thereby extending the usable spectral range and providing a resonance-enhanced regime that significantly improves the Q-factors of PE μ-antennas.

The resonance-enhanced effect observed in Fig. 4b can be interpreted from both physical and circuit perspectives. Physically, Fig. 4c displays the normalized two-dimensional stress distribution in the active region of the antenna within the operating band of the built-in FBAR. At the in-band resonance, the acoustic wave generated by the FBAR structure propagates along the y-direction, reflects within the underneath substrate, and forms a standing wave. Simultaneously, the active region of the built-in FBAR structure operates in its first mode, exhibiting a half-wavelength standing wave distribution. Figure 4d compares the stress between resonance points in and out the operating band. Within the operating band, the built-in FBAR structure forms a half-wavelength standing wave, and the substrate’s stress is lower than that of the first mode standing wave at the top, demonstrating the resonance enhancement provided by the built-in FBAR structure. In contrast, outside the operating band, the built-in FBAR structure does not operate in its resonance mode, and the stress level in the PE μ-antenna decreases by about two orders of magnitude, reflecting the absence of the resonance enhancement effect. From the circuit perspective, the Mason equivalent circuit of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna (Supplementary Fig. S5) can be described by two parallel elements: the HBAR structure and its built-in FBAR structure. Consequently, under the influence of FBAR resonance, the HBAR device exhibits an envelope peak near the thickness resonance frequency of the FBAR, consistent with the physical interpretation.

Simulation results confirm that the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits high Q-factors, with stress significantly enhanced at resonance points within the operating band due to the resonance enhancement effect. To validate this effect experimentally, we measured the HBAR-PE μ-antenna using the same gain comparison method as for the FBAR-PE μ-antenna. Figures 4e and 4f show the S parameters for the μ-antennas incorporating AlScN layers with Sc concentrations of 9.6% and 20%, respectively. The corresponding peak reflection coefficients are –2.21 dB and –8.96 dB, indicating improved impedance matching with higher Sc content. Figures 4g and 4h display the corresponding S and S curves, which 21 12 fully overlap. Within the operating band, the transmission coefficients reach their maximum levels, with each S and S peak aligning with that of the S resonance frequencies of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna. 21 12 22 These results indicate that the HBAR-PE μ-antenna follows the same acoustic-electromagnetic radiation conversion principle as the FBAR-PE μ-antenna in both transmission and reception. The resonance enhancement effect drives the built-in FBAR structure to operate in the first resonant mode at multiple in-band resonance points, increasing the stress in the ZnO layer and thereby maximizing the radiation efficiency.

The measured peak gains of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna are –28.98 dBi for the 9.6% Sc device and –26.23 dBi for the 20% Sc device, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 4 - 6.7 dBi over the FBAR-PE μ-antenna in its first mode. Since all the in-band resonances correspond to the first mode of the FBAR-PE μ-antenna, the radiation efficiencies can be evaluated based on the radiation characteristics of the first mode of FBAR, which are 0.080% and 0.156% for the 9.6% and 20% Sc devices, respectively. Consistently, the measured radiation patterns exhibit the oscillating electric-dipole characteristics of this mode (Supplementary Fig. S13), further validating the efficiency estimation. These results further confirm that the resonance enhancement effect facilitates more efficient acoustic-to- electromagnetic radiation energy conversion within the operating band. In addition, the central frequency of the operating band shifts from 2.06 GHz to 1.97 GHz, due to the reduced longitudinal acoustic velocity in the AlScN layer with higher Sc content60. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S14, the HBAR–PE μ-antenna also exhibits resonance enhancement in the second operating band, with stress again concentrated in the FBAR region. However, at these higher frequencies, the acoustic wavelength is shortened, leading to an increased number of standing waves in the substrate and reduced in-band resonance confinement. Coupled with enhanced boundary scattering and out-of-band energy leakage, these effects collectively result in a substantial reduction of the Q-factor. Consequently, the radiation gain and overall radiation efficiency in the second band of the built-in FBAR are much smaller compared to those of the first mode, rendering this band unsuitable for effective wireless signal transmission. Therefore, for practical wireless sensing applications, only the first band is employed as the operative mode of the device.

Figure 4i further demonstrates that, as the test distance increases from 10 cm to 1 m, the transmission coefficient peaks remain discernible but are reduced by an average of ~15 dB. This trend aligns with the expected free-space path loss of electromagnetic waves. The extended transmission range is attributed to the high Q factor of the HBAR-PE μ-antenna and the narrow bandwidth associated with its single resonance mode. By reducing energy dissipation and concentrating the acoustic–electrical conversion within a narrow resonance bandwidth, the high-Q HBAR structure enhances radiation intensity and improves the signal-to-noise ratio, thereby enabling more efficient long-range transmission.

ME μ-antennas have been studied by a few groups, and demonstrated its good potential for applications. To directly compare the performance of our PE μ-antennas with that of the ME μ-antennas, we also fabricated ME μ-antennas integrated on the same high-Q HBAR platform (HBAR-ME μ-antennas; the HBAR platform is characterized in Supplementary Fig. S15) to ensure identical structural configuration and acoustic propagation paths, and to minimize variations in residual stress across different material stacks. The HBAR-ME μ-antennas utilize FeGaB as the magnetostrictive layer, which exhibits a low coercive field (<0.1 mT), indicating favorable soft magnetic properties (Supplementary Fig. S16). As shown in Supplementary Fig. S17, the measured gain of the HBAR-ME μ-antennas is, on average, 3–4 dBi lower than that of their HBAR-PE counterparts, confirming the higher radiation efficiency achieved by the HBAR-PE μ-antennas. It should be noted that the resonant frequencies (Supplementary Fig. S17) of the built-in FBAR with ME antennas are higher than those (Fig. 4) of the built-in FBAR with PE antennas. This is attributed to the thinner (~645 nm) FeGaB layer with a low acoustic velocity, in contrast to the thicker (~1 μm) but high-velocity ZnO layer.

Figure 4j shows the relationship between radiation efficiency and antenna volume for the ME and PE μ-antennas with various sizes reported so far and our FBAR-PE and HBAR-PE μ-antennas. It is evident that the PE μ-antennas reduce the antenna size by 4-5 orders of magnitude and enhance radiation efficiency over 4 orders of magnitude compared to conventional piezoelectric transmitters. Notably, despite their significantly smaller size, our PE μ-antennas ultimately achieve a radiation efficiency better than or comparable to those of the state-of-the-art ME antennas34, 38, 41. This result is consistent with the comparative analysis between FBAR-PE, HBAR-PE, and ME μ-antennas, further validating the advantage of the proposed PE μ-antennas.

2.4 Wireless sensing by HBAR sensor with an integrated PE μ-antenna
The HBAR-PE μ-antenna has a higher Q factor than its FBAR-PE counterpart, enabling selectivity for frequencies with superior radiation efficiency and enhancing sensitivity for sensing. Therefore, we utilized HBAR-PE μ-antennas for wireless sensing demonstration in this work. The experimental setup for temperature and stress monitoring using HBAR sensor with integrated PE μ-antenna is illustrated in Fig. 5a. The HBAR structure, like the FBAR61, 62, is sensitive to external physical stimuli such as temperature and mechanical strain, with its frequency variation governed by the properties of the substrate materials as discussed in Supplementary Note 2. These perturbations alter the acoustic wave velocity and propagation path within the resonant cavity, resulting in a measurable shift in resonance frequency, as reflected in the S 22 parameter. As discussed earlier, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits peak radiation at resonance frequencies within the operating band of the built-in FBAR. The transmission coefficient reaches its maximum at frequencies that coincide with the μ-antenna’s resonance, establishing a one-to-one correspondence. Therefore, any shift in resonant frequency induced by stimuli will directly manifest as a shift in the transmission coefficient peak, which can be remotely detected by monitoring the position of the corresponding S or S peak at the receiving end.

For wireless temperature sensing, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna was placed on a programmable hot plate for temperature control and calibration. The horn antenna was placed at a distance away from the sensor unit (Supplementary Fig. S18). As shown in Fig. 5b for a test distance of 20 cm, the resonance peak of the μ-antenna’s S parameter exhibits a linear shift with temperature in the range of 30 ℃ to 200 ℃, with a sensitivity of –27.8 ppm/℃. Correspondingly, the peak frequencies of the received S and S signals 21 12 for the same test distance also follow a linear relationship with temperature (Fig. 5c), consistent with the S response, confirming that the PE μ-antenna can reliably transmit sensing information wirelessly. We calculated the deviation between the transmission coefficients (S and S ) shift and the S frequency 21 12 22 shift, and converted this into a temperature error using the linear relation (Figs. 5d and 5e). As the wireless transmission distance increases from 20 cm to 1 m, the sensing error increases slightly, but remaining within ±2 ℃. This deterioration is attributed to the reduced signal strength and resultant lower signal-to-noise ratio at longer distances.

Similarly, we evaluated the HBAR-PE μ-antenna as a wireless strain sensor, with calibration provided by a commercial resistive strain gauge (Supplementary Fig. S19). As shown in Fig. 5f for a test distance of 20 cm, the S resonance peaks shift linearly with applied strain in the range of 0-1000 με, 22 with a sensitivity of –0.13 ppm/με. The strain sensitivity is rather lower compared to other techniques, and is attributed to both the weak strain dependence of silicon’s longitudinal acoustic velocity and the limited sensing area, which lacks sufficient length along the deformation direction. Although the overall frequency shift due to strain variation (~261 kHz) is relatively smaller for the 20cm distance test, the peak frequencies of the S and S signals at the receiver end remain discernable and are consistent with the 21 12 μ-antenna’s resonance shifts (Fig. 5g). The wireless strain sensing error, derived by converting frequency deviation into strain values (Figs. 5h and 5i), remain within ±65 με for transmission distances up to 1 m.

Importantly, the HBAR-PE μ-antenna exhibits negligible hysteresis under both the temperature and strain sensing conditions, indicating good linearity and repeatability. These results demonstrate that the HBAR with an integrated PE μ-antenna is highly sensitive to external stimuli and the corresponding frequency shifts can be effectively transmitted and detected wirelessly with high accuracy.
